stem: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in a public subnet. The route table of the subnet sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. The instances upload files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region and download reports from a partner website on the internet. A new security rule requires that the S3 uploads travel privately and do not use the internet gateway. Access to the partner website must continue. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Access to the partner website must continue

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the subnet, and change the application to send uploads to the DNS name of the endpoint.
options.why: It works, but it adds an application change and charges, because an interface endpoint is [billed for each hour that your interface VPC endpoint is provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb).

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate it with the route table of the subnet, and keep the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway.
options.why: The endpoint route wins for this Region, because [the endpoint route takes precedence for traffic destined for the service (Amazon S3 or DynamoDB) in the current Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-beats-igw-default-route).

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, associate it with the route table of the subnet, and delete the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway.
options.why: Deleting the default route stops the website downloads, and route order does not matter, because the route table uses [longest prefix match](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-route-longest-prefix-match).

options.text: Move the instances to a private subnet, and send all their outbound traffic, including the S3 uploads, through a NAT gateway in the public subnet.
options.why: The uploads still reach the internet gateway, because [the NAT gateway must be in a public subnet with a route table that routes internet traffic to an internet gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-troubleshoot-route-placement).

explanation: A gateway endpoint adds a route whose destination is the S3 prefix list, and the route table uses [longest prefix match](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-route-longest-prefix-match), not the order of the routes. So [the endpoint route takes precedence for traffic destined for the service (Amazon S3 or DynamoDB) in the current Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-beats-igw-default-route), and other internet traffic still uses 0.0.0.0/0.
takeaway: A gateway endpoint route beats the 0.0.0.0/0 route for S3 in the same Region, because the most specific route wins.
twin: If the stem said "an S3 bucket in another AWS Region" instead: those uploads keep using the internet gateway, because [prefix lists are specific to a Region](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-beats-igw-default-route).
say: The endpoint route is more specific than the default route, so S3 traffic takes the endpoint and the rest still goes out.

stem: A company has a hybrid architecture. Servers in the company's on-premises data center connect to a VPC over an existing AWS Direct Connect connection that ends at a virtual private gateway. The servers must upload backup files to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region as the VPC. The uploads must travel privately and must not use the public internet. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Direct Connect connection that ends at a virtual private gateway

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate it with the route table of the subnets that the Direct Connect traffic enters.
options.why: The data center cannot use it, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).

options.text: Launch proxy instances in the VPC that receive the uploads from the data center and write them to Amazon S3 through a gateway endpoint.
options.why: It works, but the proxy instances add instances to patch, scale and keep available, which a managed endpoint avoids.
options.misconception: builds a proxy fleet where a managed endpoint does the job

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC, and configure the servers to send uploads to the DNS name of the endpoint.
options.why: Interface endpoints reach [services powered by PrivateLink, being AWS services, your own services or SaaS solutions](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-interface-endpoints-privatelink), and the endpoint [supports connectivity over Direct Connect](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-interface-endpoints-privatelink).

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the VPC, and route the uploads from the data center through the virtual private gateway to it.
options.why: The route fails, because you [can't route traffic to a NAT gateway from Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect using a virtual private gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-not-via-peering-or-vgw), and a NAT gateway leads to the internet.

explanation: The traffic starts outside the VPC, and [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). For those cases [you must use an interface endpoint, which is available for an additional cost](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). The interface endpoint has private IP addresses in the VPC, so the Direct Connect path reaches it.
takeaway: Traffic from on premises reaches Amazon S3 privately through an interface endpoint, not through a gateway endpoint.
twin: If the stem said "Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances download small daily updates from partner websites on the internet. The route tables of both private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone. Outbound internet access must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add a standby NAT gateway next to each one, and route each private subnet to its own zone.
options.why: It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so the standby gateways add hourly charges and no availability.

options.text: Keep the one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and keep the routes of both private subnets pointed at that NAT gateway.
options.why: If the first zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet), because the shared NAT gateway is zonal.

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet gateway, and route 0.0.0.0/0 from both private subnets to the egress-only internet gateway.
options.why: An egress-only internet gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), so the IPv4 traffic of the instances gets no path to the internet.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.
options.why: This follows the advice to [create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and configure your routing to ensure that resources use the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

explanation: Because [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), a failure of the first zone stops the shared gateway. One more gateway in the second zone, with a route per zone, removes that dependency at the lowest added cost.
takeaway: For outbound access that survives a zone failure, create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone and route each zone to its own.
twin: If the stem said "This is a test environment, and an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable." instead: keep the one NAT gateway, because each gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions).
say: One NAT gateway lives in one zone, so for a zone failure I put one in each zone and route each subnet to its own.

stem: A company runs batch workers on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones. The route tables of all private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone. Most of the traffic of the workers goes to Amazon S3 buckets in the same AWS Region, and the workers also download a significant volume of data from software repositories on the internet. The workers must stay in private subnets in all three zones. The bill shows high NAT gateway data processing charges and charges for data transfer between Availability Zones. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to reduce these charges? (Select TWO.)
keywords: Amazon S3 buckets in the same AWS Region
charges for data transfer between Availability Zones

options.text: Move the workers to public subnets, give each worker a public IPv4 address, and delete the NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone.
options.why: The workers must stay in private subnets, and [you pay an hourly rate for each public IPv4 address used by your AWS account](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-hourly-in-use-or-idle).

options.text: Associate a second Elastic IP address with the existing NAT gateway so that it can process the traffic of all three zones.
options.why: Each address adds room for [55,000 simultaneous connections](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nat-55000-connections-per-ip), but the per-gigabyte and cross-zone charges stay the same.

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate it with the route tables of all the private subnets.
options.why: [There are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge), so the S3 traffic leaves the NAT gateway.

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and send the S3 traffic of the workers to the endpoint network interfaces.
options.why: It works, but for an interface endpoint [you are also billed per GB of data processed](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb), unlike a gateway endpoint.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone that has workers, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.
options.why: For a significant volume across zones, the advice is to [create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone with resources](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-same-az-reduces-charges), which ends the cross-zone transfer.

explanation: S3 in the same Region looks free, but NAT gateway data processing applies [regardless of the traffic's source or destination](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-data-processing-any-destination). A gateway endpoint takes the S3 bytes off the NAT gateway. A NAT gateway in each zone ends the cross-zone transfer for the internet downloads.
takeaway: Cut NAT gateway bills with a gateway endpoint for S3 traffic and a NAT gateway in each zone for internet traffic.
twin: If the stem said "Amazon DynamoDB tables" instead: create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, because [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink).

stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of one VPC. Auto Scaling groups add and remove instances in three Availability Zones, and some zones have no instances for weeks. The instances need outbound IPv4 internet access that is highly available. The network team does not want to create and track a NAT gateway, a public subnet and a separate route for each Availability Zone. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: some zones have no instances for weeks
outbound IPv4 internet access that is highly available

options.text: Create one zonal NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of every private subnet to it.
options.why: The gateway is zonal, so if the first zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

options.text: Create one regional NAT gateway in manual mode, and add or remove its Availability Zones whenever the Auto Scaling groups change zones.
options.why: It works, but in manual mode [you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes).
options.misconception: chooses manual zone control where the automatic mode does the same work

options.text: Create a private NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of each private subnet to the gateway in its zone.
options.why: A private NAT gateway sends traffic [to other VPCs or on-premises networks using Transit Gateway or a virtual private gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-private-connectivity-type), not to the internet.

options.text: Create one regional NAT gateway in automatic mode, and point the 0.0.0.0/0 route of every private subnet to the regional NAT gateway.
options.why: In automatic mode [AWS automatically manages IP addresses and Availability Zone expansion](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes), so the gateway reaches new zones without work from the team.

explanation: The workloads move between zones, and the team wants no gateway or route for each zone. A regional NAT gateway has two modes. In automatic mode [AWS automatically manages IP addresses and Availability Zone expansion](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes), but in manual mode [you are responsible for expanding and contracting your NAT gateway across Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-modes). Automatic mode leaves the team one gateway to manage.
takeaway: When workloads move between zones, a regional NAT gateway in automatic mode gives highly available outbound access with one route target.
twin: If the stem said "the instances must reach other VPCs through a transit gateway, not the internet" instead: use a zonal private NAT gateway, because regional NAT gateways [do not support private NAT](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-regional-nat-no-private-nat).
say: A regional NAT gateway follows the workload across zones, so there's one gateway and one route to manage.

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer and the instances run in the same public subnets, and the instances have public IP addresses. The security groups of the load balancer and of the instances allow HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. The security team finds malicious requests that come from one known range of IP addresses. The company must allow only requests from the load balancer to reach the instances. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: allow only requests from the load balancer

options.text: Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the private IP addresses of the load balancer nodes.
options.why: It works, but [a security group can have a rule that allows traffic from another security group by its identifier, minimizing updates as resources within the group change over time](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec05-bp02-sg-references-sg), unlike node addresses.

options.text: Add an inbound rule that denies the IP address range to the network ACL of the public subnets where the load balancer runs.
options.why: The deny rule stops one range, but every other address on the internet can still reach the public IP addresses of the instances.
options.misconception: blocks one bad range when the requirement is to allow one trusted source

options.text: Replace the HTTPS rules for 0.0.0.0/0 in both security groups with allow rules for every address range except the malicious range.
options.why: The new rules still let every other address range reach the instances directly, so requests that bypass the load balancer are accepted.
options.misconception: treats removing one bad range as allowing one trusted source

options.text: Change the source of the inbound HTTPS rule in the security group of the instances to the security group of the load balancer.
options.why: A rule source can be [the ID of a security group](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-rule-sources), so the instances accept HTTPS from the load balancer and no longer from the internet.

explanation: The instances should accept requests from the load balancer alone. A security group rule can take [the ID of a security group](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-rule-sources) as its source, and the example web tier [allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg) this way. After the 0.0.0.0/0 source is replaced, direct requests from the internet match no allow rule.
takeaway: To accept traffic from one tier alone, name the security group of that tier as the source of the rule.
twin: If the stem said "The company must prevent all requests from that range from reaching the application." instead: add a deny rule to the network ACL, because [network ACLs can be used to set both Allow and Deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only).
say: I'd make the load balancer's security group the only source in the instances' security group.

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances download small daily updates from partner websites on the internet. The route tables of both private subnets send 0.0.0.0/0 to one NAT gateway in a public subnet in the first Availability Zone. This is a test environment, and an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: an outage of one Availability Zone is acceptable

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each zone, add a standby NAT gateway next to each one, and route each private subnet to its own zone.
options.why: It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so the standbys add cost.

options.text: Keep the one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and keep the routes of both private subnets pointed at that NAT gateway.
options.why: The stem accepts a zone outage, and for test you can [save money by deploying your resources in only one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-dev-test-one-az-saves-money), so one gateway is enough.

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with an egress-only internet gateway, and route 0.0.0.0/0 from both private subnets to the egress-only internet gateway.
options.why: An egress-only internet gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), so the IPv4 traffic of the instances gets no path to the internet.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.
options.why: It works, but a second gateway adds a second hourly charge, because a NAT gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions).
options.misconception: builds zone redundancy into a test environment that accepts a zone outage

explanation: The stem accepts the loss of one zone and asks for the lowest cost. A NAT gateway is [charged for each hour that your NAT gateway is available](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions) and for [each gigabyte of data that it processes](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-pricing-dimensions), so every extra gateway adds an hourly charge. The traffic is small, so the existing gateway is the cheapest design that works.
takeaway: In a test environment that accepts a zone outage, one shared NAT gateway is the cheapest working design.
twin: If the stem said "Outbound internet access must stay highly available during an Availability Zone failure." instead: add a second NAT gateway, because [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).
say: It's a test environment and a zone outage is fine, so one NAT gateway is the cheapest choice.
